hints: Start from the formula $\text{Mg}_2\text{Si}$ and work out how many electrons each Mg atom must lose and how many the Si atom must gain to reach a noble gas octet.
Think about what charge and outer electron count each resulting ion will have, and how to show two identical magnesium ions with one silicon ion.
walkthrough:
Work out the electron transfer**
Magnesium is in Group 2, so each Mg atom has 2 outer electrons to lose. Silicon is in Group 14, so a Si atom needs 4 more electrons to complete its octet. That is why two Mg atoms each give 2 electrons to one Si atom, giving $2\text{Mg}^{2+} + \text{Si}^{4-}$.

Draw the ions correctly**
Show each $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ separately with its charge outside brackets and with no dots or crosses left in the outer shell. Show the $\text{Si}^{4-}$ in brackets with 8 electrons around it, all from the magnesium atoms so shown as crosses (or dots), with a $4-$ charge outside. That arrangement represents one formula unit of $\text{Mg}_2\text{Si}$.

Final answer: Two $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions shown with no outer electrons (or with 8 electrons in previous shell) and one $\text{Si}^{4-}$ ion shown with 8 outer electrons.
Charges shown as $2+$ on each Mg and $4-$ on Si.

hints: List the reactants $\text{Mg}_2\text{Si}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and the products $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ and $\text{SiH}_4$, then count Mg, Si, H and O atoms on each side.
Decide the physical state of each substance from the description: solid silicide, liquid water, aqueous magnesium hydroxide solution and gaseous silane.
walkthrough:
Balance the atoms**
You have $\text{Mg}_2\text{Si} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2 + \text{SiH}_4$. There are 2 Mg on the left, so you need $2\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ on the right. That gives 4 O and 4 H in the hydroxide plus 4 H in silane, so 8 H and 4 O in total on the right. Therefore you need $4\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the left.

Add the state symbols**
Solid $\text{Mg}_2\text{Si}$ is (s). Water as a liquid reactant is (l). Magnesium hydroxide is described as a solution, so (aq). Silane is described as a gas, so (g). Put them all together to give $$\text{Mg}_2\text{Si(s)} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow 2\text{Mg(OH)}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{SiH}_4\text{(g)}$$

hints: Decide whether $\text{SiH}_4$ exists as separate small molecules or as a giant lattice, and what type of bonding holds each molecule together internally.
Identify the only forces that can act between separate neutral $\text{SiH}_4$ molecules and how strong they are, linking this to energy needed to separate them.
walkthrough:
Picture what SiH4 really is**
Inside each $\text{SiH}_4$ the Si and H atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds, but between one $\text{SiH}_4$ and the next there are no covalent or ionic bonds. It is a collection of separate, small neutral molecules, a simple molecular structure.

Link weak attractions to being a gas**
Between neutral molecules the only attractions are very weak temporary induced dipole-dipole forces. Only a tiny amount of thermal energy is needed to overcome them, so $\text{SiH}_4$ boils well below room temperature and exists as a gas.

Final answer: $\text{SiH}_4$ has a simple molecular structure.
Only weak induced dipole-dipole (London dispersion) forces exist between molecules, so little energy is needed to separate them, giving a low boiling point and a gas at room temperature.

hints: Compare the electronegativity numbers: C is 2.5, H is 2.1 and Si is 1.8, and recall that the more electronegative atom gains the $\delta-$ charge.
Check the direction of the difference for C-H versus Si-H, noting that Si is less electronegative than H while C is more electronegative than H.
walkthrough:
Assign C-H polarity**
Carbon at 2.5 pulls electrons more strongly than hydrogen at 2.1. So the bonding electrons sit closer to C, giving $$\text{C}^{\delta-}-\text{H}^{\delta+}$$

Assign Si-H polarity in the opposite sense**
Silicon at 1.8 is less electronegative than hydrogen at 2.1, so hydrogen now pulls harder. The dipole reverses to give $$\text{Si}^{\delta+}-\text{H}^{\delta-}$$ The differences are small, so both are described as weak dipoles.

Final answer: $\text{C}^{\delta-}-\text{H}^{\delta+}$
$\text{Si}^{\delta+}-\text{H}^{\delta-}$

hints: Recall the shape of methane from four bonding pairs and no lone pairs on carbon, and picture where the four H atoms point in space.
Think about what happens when four identical weak bond dipoles point equally in opposite directions in a highly symmetrical molecule.
walkthrough:
Fix the shape in your mind**
Methane has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs around C, so it is tetrahedral with bond angles of about $109.5^{\circ}$. All four C-H bonds are identical and point to the corners of a tetrahedron.

See why the dipoles cancel**
Each C-H bond is weakly polar, but because the tetrahedron is perfectly symmetrical the pull in one direction is exactly balanced by pulls in the other directions. The vector sum is zero, so the molecule as a whole is nonpolar with no overall dipole moment.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_4$ is tetrahedral.
The four identical C-H bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically and cancel, so there is no overall dipole moment.

hints: Compare bond breaking at the start of combustion: which bond must break, $\text{Si-H}$ or $\text{C-H}$, and which is longer and weaker using Data Booklet values.
Link weaker bonds to the energy barrier for reaction, recalling that less energy needed to start breaking bonds means a lower activation energy.
walkthrough:
Compare the bonds that must break**
Both combustions need X-H bonds to break in the first step. Silicon is larger than carbon, so $\text{Si-H}$ is longer and much weaker than $\text{C-H}$. Data Booklet values show $\text{Si-H}$ around $320 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ compared with $\text{C-H}$ around $410 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Connect bond strength to ignition**
Breaking weaker $\text{Si-H}$ bonds needs less initial energy, so the activation energy barrier is low. Collisions at room temperature already provide enough energy, so $\text{SiH}_4$ bursts into flame in air. The stronger $\text{C-H}$ bonds give a higher activation energy, so $\text{CH}_4$ needs a spark or flame to get started.

Final answer: $\text{Si-H}$ bond is much weaker than $\text{C-H}$ bond.
Less energy is needed to break $\text{Si-H}$, so activation energy for $\text{SiH}_4$ oxidation is low enough to be provided by room temperature, while $\text{CH}_4$ needs ignition.

hints: Recall the general reaction of an acidic oxide with a strong alkali: it forms a salt plus water, similar to $\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH}$.
Work out the silicon containing sodium salt from $\text{SiO}_2$ and $\text{NaOH}$, keeping the Si to O ratio in mind.
walkthrough:
Recognise the pattern**
$\text{SiO}_2$ is an acidic oxide, so with hot concentrated $\text{NaOH}$ it is neutralised like $\text{CO}_2$ gives a carbonate. Here the salt keeps one Si, giving sodium silicate.

Name both products**
The balanced equation is $$\text{SiO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ So the two products are sodium silicate, $\text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3$, and water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Final answer: sodium silicate, $\text{Na}_2\text{SiO}_3$
water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Recall what term describes an oxide that reacts with a base or alkali to form a salt and water.
walkthrough:
Label the behaviour**
Because $\text{SiO}_2$ reacts with a strong base to give a salt plus water and does not react with acids in the same way, it is behaving as an acidic oxide.
Final answer: acidic (oxide behaviour)
